# Pre-mortem: Dispatch as one graph of typed nodes and tuples

Red team of Sami's direction (direct message to the INFRA Legion controller, 2026-11-04 06:55Z, `77e56cd3-4efd-433d-916c-81ec36281aae`): model everything in Dispatch internally as nodes with typed relations, Tana-style, without exposing supertags to users yet.

Read-only. Repository facts are from `github.com/cybermonklabs/legion` at commit `3bf3468ddeee400b85ddb5eff2975885155a5db9`, paths relative to `packages/envoy/internal/dispatch` unless stated. `[inference]` marks reasoning rather than reading.

## Verdict (confidence: high)

The model is right and it is already half-built. What will kill it is the word *rewrite*. Dispatch's graph today is a **derived view**, not a store: `graph_edges` is a 25-arm `union all` over `refs`, `issues`, `issue_links`, `artifacts`, `asks`, `comments`, `messages`, `ask_followers`, `components`, `document_blocks`, `block_refs`, `comment_blocks`, `message_blocks`, `ask_blocks` and their ref tables (`store/migrations/20261101183525_graph_edges_ask_parts_and_block_pointers.up.sql`). Typed relations already exist in a narrow form: `plan_task.serves` and `check.serves` are attributes of kind `block[]` with `targets: ["requirement"]` in `pmdoc/schema/blocks.json` (schema version 3), and the view filters them with `block_ref_listed(to_types, to_id)`.

So the right move is **not** a new graph database and not a migration of live rows. It is: one writer per fact, nodes and edges derived from it, and one query replaced at a time behind a shadow diff. Everything below is what goes wrong if that discipline slips.

## Risk 0, the most likely of all: the rewrite eats the quarter and no user sees anything

INFRA-156 was approved at spec v16, produced 6 of 8 children, hit `review_round_cap=3` (message `3f3fdbd2`, 2026-10-30), and parked other work: INFRA-449 and INFRA-450 were put in backlog "waiting for the graph rewrite, dispatch://INFRA-156". A year later the honest failure is not a corrupted database; it is twelve merged PRs of plumbing, two tabs that look the same, and Sami's original friction — too many ways to touch the same data — untouched.

- **Early warning:** a third issue parked "until the graph lands"; a graph PR whose acceptance names no user-visible behaviour; children splitting into sub-children (Sami's own oversplit complaint, same message).
- **Prevention:** a standing rule — *no feature issue may block on the graph, and every graph slice ships one visible change*. One graph slice in flight at a time. If a slice cannot name the screen or the command that changes, it is not a slice.

## The ten ways it goes wrong

### 1\. Live-data migration: two indexers, one truth, permanent drift

Blocks are indexed by triggers plus a drain queue: `block_grammar_owed` with `block_grammar_owe()` (`store/migrations/0121_block_graph.up.sql`), `document_block_versions` with a null version meaning *owed*, and `document_indexed_versions` recording which versions a block-aware build actually read. The INFRA-156 retro already named this shape as a hazard: `docs/solutions/architecture-patterns/two-paths-that-index-one-document*` (message `6671eca4` on INFRA-156, 2026-10-30). A node/edge table written *beside* the existing tables makes that two paths for every kind, not just documents.

- **Early warning:** the first "reconcile nodes" or "rebuild graph" script; a bug fixed in the comment path but not the node path; an owed queue that never drains to zero.
- **Prevention:** never dual-write. Nodes and edges stay derived — a view, or a table written only by the existing indexer inside the same transaction as the source row. Keep the `.census.sql` convention (every migration carries one) as a continuous equality check: count and digest rows per kind, source versus graph, alert on any difference. Backfill through the owed-queue pattern already proven, never a big `UPDATE`.

### 2\. The read cliff: one generic query over a 25-arm union

"Every message to me is a query on that graph" over `graph_edges` means the planner evaluates every arm, several of them multi-way joins (`component_depends`, `issue_component_members`, the ask/comment/message block-ref joins). Today's inbox does not do this: `user_threads` is a materialised per-login table with `user_threads_unread (login, replied_at desc, thread_id desc) where unread` (`store/migrations/0095_user_threads.up.sql`), maintained by trigger and seeded by `0098_user_threads_seed.up.sql`. Replacing an indexed table read with a union scan is the kind of regression that only appears on real data.

- **Early warning:** any inbox p99 above today's; a `materialized view` or planner hint appearing in a PR; `explain` output with a sequential scan on `comments` or `messages`.
- **Prevention:** keep the derived read models. The graph is the *model*; `user_threads`-shaped projections stay the *index*. Set the budget before the first PR (inbox p99 ≤ today's, measured with the existing harness — `TestTheOutboxLoadSteps`, `outbox/THROUGHPUT.md`) and fail the PR on it.

### 3\. Search regresses while costing more

INFRA-156 R13 replaces per-item embedding with windows of neighbouring blocks, each a few hundred tokens, with the title and heading as context; the queue paces at 200,000 estimated tokens a minute (`embedqueue/queue.go`), and the vector table grows from one row per item to one row per window. Production has no embedder configured at all, so search there matches words only (INFRA-194).

- **Early warning:** an embed backlog that never empties after a deploy; a jump in embedding spend; hits that name blocks but read worse than the old item-level results.
- **Prevention:** re-embed only windows whose text or context changed (R13 says this; hold acceptance A9 to it). Keep the keyword path as the floor and A/B the block-window ranker against it on a fixed query set before it becomes the default. Treat "search got worse" as a release blocker, not a follow-up.

### 4\. A person is not a node, so Sami's query cannot be written

This is the structural gap, and nothing in INFRA-156 closes it. `graph_edges` has node kinds issue, artifact, block, comment_block, message_block, ask_block, ask, comment, message, component, session — and **no person**. People live in JSON actor fields (`author->>'kind' = 'user'`, `lower(author->>'id')` in `api/unread_replies.go`), and the only actor-like edge is `followed_by` to a *session*. Worse, identity is deliberately split: the read mark is keyed on the canonical login and the Clear on the raw actor id, "the deliberate asymmetry between 0048's convention and 0033's, which nothing here is free to swap" (`api/unread_replies.go`).

- **Early warning:** a graph PR that adds relations between content nodes but still resolves people with `lower(author->>'id')`; a second canonicalisation helper.
- **Prevention:** make `person` a node kind and `authored_by` / `addressed_to` / `delivered_to` real edges, written by the code that already computes them, *before* any "query over the graph" is written. One canonicalisation function, one alias table (canonical login, raw actor id, sessions, roles). Identity aliasing is the first supertag, not an afterthought.

### 5\. The unified inbox silently drops people's mail

"Every thread I'm in is a query" hides a lot of earned behaviour: thread-root walks with a depth bound and a cycle guard because `comments.reply_to` has no acyclicity constraint, document credits (creator plus every version's authors), mention precedence (`destinations.leftToMention`), role forwards, claimants and routes, and the actor filtered out of their own event (`outbox/recipients.go`); plus read marks, Clear and per-reply read rows (`user_agent_read`, `user_agent_state`, `user_agent_reply_read`). A naive "all nodes related to me" reproduces the addition rules and loses the subtraction rules.

- **Early warning:** a spec sentence of the form "the inbox is one query" with no clause for read state or mention precedence; the first "I stopped getting X" report after a deploy.
- **Prevention:** build the graph inbox as a **second** implementation behind a flag and shadow-diff it against the live Inbox+Replies for a week per user, counting mismatches by cause. Cut over after three days at zero. Never delete `user_threads` in the PR that adds the query.

### 6\. Block identity under Yjs: citations go dangling at the rate people type

The dashboard edits documents with Yjs (`yjs ^13.6.32`, `y-protocols ^1.0.6` in `packages/dispatch/package.json`); the server validates and stores the updates (`docs/websocket.go`). INFRA-156 R11/A13 require ids to survive reword, move, split (the part holding the start keeps the id) and join, and a body sent without ids to be matched by text. Once decisions, checks and inbox entries all point at blocks, every concurrent edit can break a tuple someone's audit trail depends on, and reconnecting offline editors replay old intents.

- **Early warning:** a rising count of links resolving to a removed block; "changed since cited" on blocks nobody edited; the text-matching fallback firing on dashboard edits (it should only fire for API bodies).
- **Prevention:** ids assigned and validated server-side at save, never trusted from a client; the staleness rule already shipped — `text_sha256` plus `changed_version` (`document_blocks`, `check_results`, and `POST .../keep` answering 409 `DECISION_CHANGED`) — applied to every typed relation; edges to deleted blocks *marked removed*, never garbage-collected (R4/A2); a dangling-citation counter on the dashboard from day one.

### 7\. Type sprawl, and a schema that cannot evolve

`blocks.json` is compiled into both server and web app (`contracts/src/block-schema.generated.ts`), so a new type is a PR plus a deploy, and a schema-version bump puts open editors read-only until reload (INFRA-682/spec). That rigidity is today's safety rail. Tana-style supertags remove it; then agents invent `decision`, `decision_record` and `Decision`, attributes drift (`owner` versus `assignee`), and migrations become data nobody reviews. Sami is right to keep supertags internal — the risk is that "internal" quietly becomes "runtime-defined".

- **Early warning:** more than roughly three new types in a month; two attributes with one meaning and two names; the first request to define a type from the UI "just for this issue".
- **Prevention:** one registry generating Go and TypeScript types (already planned: INFRA-525 folded into INFRA-173), a reserved vocabulary with human naming review, and a written deprecation path (rename with alias, rewrite, drop) exercised end to end *before* the sixth type ships.

### 8\. Permissions: a generic graph is a generic authorization hole

Auth today is four route modes — `authPublic`, `authAny`, `authHuman`, `authBearer` (`api/routes_table.go:17-26`) — each route carrying its own scope checks, and agents authenticate with a *deployment-wide shared* bearer (`DISPATCH_AGENT_TOKEN`, `auth/agent_token.go`): every agent is the same principal. One `/api/v1/graph/query` endpoint would let any agent traverse to anything, including direct messages, which INFRA-156 deliberately leaves unaddressable ("Direct messages still have no `dispatch://` address").

- **Early warning:** a PR proposing a filter or query language over nodes; a node kind reachable by traversal that no route exposes directly; a test that catches cross-project reads and is then "fixed" by updating the expectation.
- **Prevention:** no general query endpoint. Named, versioned queries only, each with its own auth mode and scope test. One visibility predicate per node kind that the query layer cannot bypass, with a test that enumerates kinds and fails when a new kind has none. Per-session agent tokens before any cross-kind traversal is exposed (the Airlock direction, INFRA-1121).

### 9\. The graph lags the notification: "I got pinged, my inbox is empty"

Reads already have a safe-horizon rule (`GET /api/v1/references?since=` reads "up to the event log's safe horizon"), block grammar is indexed from an owed queue, and the outbox publishes to NATS/Envoy on its own path at a measured rate (`outbox/THROUGHPUT.md`). If the inbox becomes a derived graph query while notifications stay event-driven, the two skew under load — and the skew shows exactly when the system is busiest.

- **Early warning:** owed-queue depth or outbox lag with no alert; a report pairing a notification with an empty view; test flakes fixed by sleeping.
- **Prevention:** serve the inbox read from the same horizon the events use, so a notification can never precede its node. Export queue depth and horizon lag as metrics with alerts. Guarantee read-your-writes for the author's own write (the event feed already invalidates queries: `web/src/api/event-feed.ts`).

### 10\. Agents and skills break mid-flight

The API is large (≈300 routes in `api/routes_table.go`) and agents reach it through the `dispatch` CLI, `packages/contracts` and skills that teach exact commands. Renaming `comment` to `node`, or changing `GET /api/v1/issues/{key}/decisions` in place, breaks running sessions mid-task, not just future ones.

- **Early warning:** a plan that renames fields on existing routes; a skill PR that must merge in the same window as a server deploy; a client carrying its own copy of a server rule (the length-cap mistake INFRA-151 recorded).
- **Prevention:** additive only. New node routes beside the old; old response shapes served from the new model; INFRA-156's rolling-deploy acceptance (A12: each build answers every read it supports and skips edges of kinds it does not know) applied to every slice. Skills change only after the server has served both shapes for a week.

## What a world-class implementation looks like

The pattern that works is **tuples as the internal log, typed read models at the edges, a closed schema, named queries.**

- **Datomic** (verified 2026-11-04, https://docs.datomic.com/datomic-overview.html): a database is a set of immutable datoms `[E A V Tx op]`; transactions add, never update; four indexes (EAVT, AEVT, AVET, VAET) serve row, column, key-value and graph access; "as-of" queries come free. Its stated tradeoff is the one to handle deliberately: *"No structural 'types' … all entities have the same universal type"*, so there is no declarative way to say "a person must have a name". Dispatch needs those structural rules: tuple log underneath, closed schema on top.
- **Tana** — supertags give a node a type and fields, and live queries are the UI; the direction Sami names. Take the model, not the exposure (https://tana.inc, help.tana.inc; *not fetched in this session*).
- **Notion** — every block has an id, a parent and a type, databases are typed collections, backlinks per page; also the counter-example that it still keeps comments outside the document, as INFRA-156's own prior-art study records (dispatch://INFRA-156/artifact/prior-art-md).
- **Roam / Logseq** — block-level references work as a daily driver; Logseq's move to a real database for its DB version is the performance lesson. **RDF/SPARQL versus property graphs (openCypher/Neo4j)** — RDF needs reification (or RDF-star) to put properties on an edge, a property graph does not, so store edge attributes natively. **TerminusDB** — the closest prior art for schema-as-data with commits and migration operations. (*Sources not fetched in this session.*)

Concretely for Dispatch: one append-only edge table carrying `(from_node, kind, to_node, created_at, source_seq, actor)`, written only by existing indexers; `graph_edges` kept as the compatibility view; projections such as `user_threads` as the latency layer; a generated schema registry; and a small set of named queries, each authorized per kind.

## The smallest first slice that proves the model

Two queries, one shared foundation; roughly two weeks of one worker. Both already exist in another form, so the diff is measurable.

**Foundation (days 1-3).** `person` as a node kind with one alias table (canonical login, raw actor id, sessions, roles) wrapping the existing canonicalisation; `authored_by` and `delivered_to` edges derived inside the recipient computation that already runs (`outbox/recipients.go`). No route changes. Acceptance: for every comment, message and ask of the last 30 days, the derived edge set equals what the current recipient code returns — a census query, zero differences.

**Slice A — Decisions as nodes (days 4-8).** Today the Decisions tab parses a document: "Each decision is one `##` section of that document" (`api/decisions.go:19-22`, `decisionsDocumentName = "decisions.md"`). Add a `decision` block type to `blocks.json` (version 4) with relations `shaped` (`block[]`, targeting spec blocks), `from_ask` (ask) and `decided_by` (actor), reusing the `block[]` machinery `plan_task.serves` already uses. `GET /api/v1/issues/{key}/decisions` answers from nodes where they exist and from the document parse otherwise — same JSON, same `text_sha256` and Keep 409 rule. Acceptance: the existing `decisions_test.go` fixtures pass unchanged against the node path; one real issue shows each decision with the spec blocks it shaped and the ask that caused it; no client change.

**Slice B — the inbox as one query (days 9-14).** `GET /api/v1/me/inbox` reading nodes where `delivered_to = me`, joined to `user_threads` for read state, replies listed as ordinary nodes. Ship it dark: shadow-diff against the live Inbox+Replies for every active user, mismatches counted by cause on a visible page. Cut over after three consecutive days at zero; `user_threads` stays.

**Kill criteria.** If Slice A cannot reproduce today's Decisions JSON within a week, the typed-relation layer is not as reusable as it looks and the model needs rework before anything is built on it. If Slice B's shadow diff does not converge in a week, the inbox's subtraction rules are not yet expressible as a query: keep the projection and stop.

**What success proves:** that a decision, a message and a reply are one kind of thing with different relations, that one query serves a person's whole world, and that neither cost a single breaking change to an agent.

Renaming `comment` to `node`, or changing `GET /api/v1/issues/{key}/decisions` in place, breaks running sessions mid-task, not just future ones.

- **Early warning:** a plan that renames fields on existing routes; a skill PR that must merge in the same window as a server deploy; a client carrying its own copy of a server rule (the length-cap mistake INFRA-151 recorded).
- **Prevention:** additive only. New node routes beside the old; old response shapes served from the new model; INFRA-156's rolling-deploy acceptance (A12: each build answers every read it supports and skips edges of kinds it does not know) applied to every slice. Skills change only after the server has served both shapes for a week.
